name: Scope insensitivity
statement: People are said to state the same price for saving 2,000 things as for saving 200,000, but most split-sample surveys that vary quantity do find a difference.
meaning: The claim is about what a stated valuation tracks. Ask one group what it would pay to fix a problem, ask a matched group the same question with the problem ten or a hundred times larger, and the two answers are held to come out the same. If that were general, a survey-based value would measure the topic rather than the amount, and any figure derived from one could be set by whoever wrote the questionnaire. Economists call the comparison a scope test, and the term comes from the 1993 NOAA panel that reviewed the method after the Exxon Valdez spill. Three explanations compete. Kahneman and Knetsch argued that respondents are buying moral satisfaction, a warm glow whose size does not depend on how much good the money does. Baron and Greene argued for prominence, that the type of good is easy to attend to and its quantity is not. Contingent-valuation practitioners argued that flat answers come from bad instruments, and that a survey which holds attention produces answers that move.

origin.who: William H. Desvousges, F. Reed Johnson, Richard W. Dunford, Kevin J. Boyle, Sara P. Hudson and K. Nicole Wilson
origin.note: The monograph carries a 1992 Exxon Corporation copyright and was written while RTI was retained by Exxon during the Exxon Valdez litigation. It appeared as an institutional monograph rather than in a journal. RTI Press reissued it in 2010 with the original text unchanged and no new analyses. Kahneman and Knetsch published their embedding paper the same year, and the word scope entered the debate a year later through the NOAA panel.

evidence: The bird experiment ran in two Atlanta shopping malls between 17 May and 5 June 1991. Recruiters intercepted adults over 19 who were not full-time students, and the questionnaires were self-administered, with 1,205 completed across the three migratory-waterfowl versions. Respondents read that waterfowl drown in uncovered waste-oil holding ponds in the Central Flyway, and were asked the most their household would agree to pay each year in higher prices for wire-net covers. The only difference between versions was the number of birds. Protest zeros, outliers and responses above a quarter of income were dropped. Table 5-1 then gives mean willingness to pay of $80 for 2,000 birds, $78 for 20,000 and $88 for 200,000, with N of 288, 286 and 281 and a median of $25 in all three. Wilcoxon rank sum tests gave p-values of 0.178, 0.457 and 0.145 for the three pairwise comparisons. Tobit models put the predicted means at $59, $59 and $71 under a linear specification and $81, $80 and $123 under a log specification. A second experiment in the same monograph asked about preventing damage from small oil spills or from all oil spills, and the larger programme drew a lower mean, $95 against $144. Kahneman and Knetsch ran a different design. Three telephone samples in greater Vancouver, of 66, 78 and 74 adults, were asked to price public services at nested levels of inclusiveness. Median willingness to pay for the first good named was $25 at the narrowest level and $50 at the two wider ones, a difference their Mann-Whitney test did not find. Asked instead to allocate down from a broader total, the same rescue-equipment good drew a median of $1.00 in their Table I. The running text gives that figure as $1.50 and the ratio as about 16, so the paper disagrees with its own table. In a separate survey of 14 nested pairs of causes, rank correlations between mean moral-satisfaction ratings and median willingness to pay were 0.78 and 0.62. Baron and Greene ran 11 experiments, on students at the University of Pennsylvania and on adults stopped in Philadelphia's main railway station, and reported that contribution, warm glow and budget constraints did not fit the data, while prominence did.

replication.headline: The bird result held when the same questionnaire was rerun aloud with an interviewer present, and failed to appear in the large surveys that vary quantity under better conditions.
replication.detail: Schkade and Payne put the Desvousges questionnaire and its three treatments through a think-aloud protocol with an interviewer in the room. Carson reports that their conference paper gave an analysis of variance p-value of 0.42 on willingness to pay and their journal paper 0.18 on the log of willingness to pay, so by their own test the flat pattern reproduced. Carson also prints their cell figures, means of $84.23, $62.47 and $121.82 on 28, 29 and 30 respondents, medians $25, $30 and $50, and shows that a one-sided regression of log willingness to pay on bird numbers rejects the flat null at p < 0.05. Those cell figures are Carson's reading of their data rather than this entry's reading of their paper. Carson's own survey of the literature counted 19 studies of goods with substantial passive use, and over 30 studies in total, in which the hypothesis of insensitivity to scope was rejected at p < 0.10, against a handful where it was not. The largest test since is the survey commissioned for the Deepwater Horizon assessment. Bishop and 19 colleagues drew a random sample of households across the contiguous United States and completed face-to-face interviews with 3,656 people between October 2013 and July 2014, at a weighted response rate of 48%. Respondents were randomised to a smaller or a larger set of injuries at one of five tax amounts. Support fell as the tax rose and rose with the size of the injury set at every tax amount, 57.7% against 52.2% at $15 and 28.1% against 24.2% at $435. Lower-bound mean willingness to pay came out at $136 with a standard error of $6.34 for the smaller set and $153 with a standard error of $6.87 for the larger.

K., Tourangeau, R., Welsh, M., Wooldridge, J. M., DeBell, M., Donovan, C., Konopka, M., & Scherer, N. (2017). Putting a value on injuries to natural assets: The BP oil spill. Science, 356(6335), 253-254.

limits: Passing a scope test is not the whole question, and both camps now say so. Desvousges, Mathews and Train assembled 109 contingent-valuation studies that ran scope tests and found that only three permit any judgement of whether the size of the response was adequate rather than merely non-zero. Their paper was supported in part by BP. Their worked example is Chapman and colleagues, whose respondents valued a package of three river and lake improvements at $184 and one of its components, offered on top of another, at $138. Desvousges and colleagues call that response demonstrably inadequate, and say any positive discount rate widens the gap. Chapman, Bishop, Hanemann, Kanninen, Krosnick, Morey and Tourangeau answered in the same journal, and Train replied two pages later. Whitehead answers with scope elasticity, the proportional change in willingness to pay per proportional change in quantity. His simulation of plausible willingness-to-pay functions gives a mean elasticity of 0.927 under a linear form and 0.708 under a quadratic one. He reports that every elasticity he recovers falls in that range, and that where a confidence interval can be built the elasticity differs from zero but not from one. The qualifier carries weight, because one of his own estimates, from a model with covariates, has an interval running from below zero to above one. Desvousges and colleagues report that Heberlein, Wilson, Bishop and Schaeffer go further and would drop the standard scope test altogether, and that paper could not be read here. Almost every headline figure on this page was produced by someone retained in oil-spill litigation, on one side or the other. The wider literature is not so placed, and the studies Carson lists are mostly other people's work, on horse farms, waiting times and sea turtles. Schkade and Payne's own paper could not be obtained either, so what this page reports of it is Carson's account. Crossref, CORE and a plain search on 21 September 2026 found no preregistered replication of Baron and Greene and no multi-laboratory project covering the effect, so the psychology outside contingent valuation stays thinner than the economics. Proportion dominance sits at entry 193, insensitivity to sample size at 229, compassion fade at 232, the identifiable victim effect at 179 and extension neglect at 549.
misreadings: The famous numbers are real. Desvousges and colleagues do print $80, $78 and $88, in Table 5-1 of the monograph, and the retellings quote them correctly. What the retellings drop is the wording. All three versions told respondents the deaths were a share of 8.5 million birds in the Central Flyway, described as much less than 1 percent, less than 1 percent, and about 2 percent. A respondent reading the 200,000 version saw a problem twice the size of a small one, not a hundred times the size. The setting is also usually wrong. There was no oil spill and no Alaska in the questionnaire, only uncovered waste-oil holding ponds in the middle of the country, and the survey ran in shopping malls in Atlanta. Carson's own chapter places the ponds in the Rocky Mountain states. Second, the monograph's authors did not rest on the raw means. Their Tobit log specification gave $81, $80 and $123, and the 200,000 comparisons under it were significant at the 10 percent level, which they set aside because the linear models fitted better. A likelihood-ratio test rejected equality of the coefficient vectors across versions, so the same answers were being generated by different processes. Carson, refitting their 10 percent trimmed data, found willingness to pay rising with the share of birds saved at p = 0.001, and still counted the study as evidence for insensitivity given how it was administered. Third, Kahneman and Knetsch did not run the bird study and their 1992 paper contains no bird counts. Their subject was embedding, the finding that the same good is priced differently depending on how wide a category the question opens with. Attributing the birds to them, or the moral-satisfaction argument to Desvousges, merges two papers that share a year and nothing else.
